en.title: Chad Powers Season 2: Glen Powell's Wild Scheme Continues
en.summary: The utterly ridiculous premise of **Chad Powers** returns for a second season, doubling down on its charm and absurdity. Glen Powell is back as Russ Holliday and his football-playing alter ego, proving that some things are just too fun to mess with.
en.body:
The premise of **Chad Powers** is, to put it mildly, delightfully bonkers. We're still deep in the world of Russ Holliday, a quarterback whose career imploded, now attempting a comeback through a meticulously crafted disguise: his wig- and prosthetics-powered alter ego, Chad Powers. Season two, which dropped on Hulu on September 3, 2026, doesn't shy away from this inherent silliness; in fact, it leans into it with infectious enthusiasm. This season, the core conflict shifts. While the ever-present tension of being discovered still simmers, the narrative focus now centers on the machimsions of backup QB Gerry (played by **Colton Ryan**), whose growing envy and suspicion of Chad threaten to unravel everything.

Crucially, Coach Hudson's daughter and Russ's love interest, Ricky Hudson (a fantastic **Perry Mattfeld**), is now in on the secret. This changes the game, moving the stakes from 'Will he get caught?' to 'How will this complicated web of deception and affection untangle?' The early episodes might feel like a comfortable continuation of season one's flavor, but the pacing soon picks up, delivering laughs and surprisingly heartfelt moments. One standout scene involving Russ's dad, played by **Toby Huss**, in the "10th Quarter" is a masterclass in escalating humor from a jump-scare to pure hilarity, underscored by genuine emotion.

## A Familiar, Yet Funnier, Return

The genius of **Chad Powers** lies in its refusal to reinvent the wheel. Unlike shows that constantly pivot their core concept, this series understands its strengths and doubles down. Glen Powell, reprising his titular role, is even better in his second outing. His performance is a tightrope walk between hapless jock and cunning imposter, and he navigates it with impeccable comedic timing and surprising depth. The supporting cast also shines, making the outlandish situations feel grounded in relatable character dynamics. The show’s humor is sharp, often relying on the absurdity of the central conceit and the characters' reactions to it.

## The Chad Powers Fan Phenomenon

Fans of **Chad Powers** have embraced the show's unique blend of sports comedy and identity farce. The series has cultivated a passionate following who appreciate its willingness to be unabashedly silly while still telling a compelling story. The second season, with its refined conflicts and expanded character arcs, has only deepened this connection. Viewers are invested not just in Chad's potential downfall, but in the genuine relationships forming amidst the chaos. The show’s ability to elicit both belly laughs and genuine emotional responses has cemented its status as a fan favorite, proving that sometimes, more of the same—especially when it's this good—is exactly what the audience wants.

## What's Next

While season two has just premiered, the series finale reportedly swaps one antagonist for another, hinting at future narrative shifts without jeopardizing the core premise. Fans can anticipate more of the signature humor and character-driven storylines that have made **Chad Powers** a hit. Specific details about season three have not yet been announced.

content_raw: The premise of the Glen Powell vehicle “ Chad Powers ” is ridiculous and doesn’t get any less so in season two. This is still a show about Russ Holliday, an epic flame-out of a quarterback, and his attempt to regain the spotlight as his wig- and prosthetics-powered alter ego, Chad Powers. Yes, in season two, assistant coach, coach’s daughter, and Chad/Russ’s love interest Ricky Hudson (Perry Mattfeld) knows about the deception. And the central conflict is less about whether Russ can pull it off (although the tension of getting caught still hangs over everything) and more about what trouble backup QB Gerry ( Colton Ryan ) can stir up as his envy and suspicion of Chad grow. Which is to say season two is remarkably like season one, same tone, same conflicts, same humor—with only the smallest of adjustments. The first episode feels like it could have been plucked from the middle of the first installment, extending the flavor of the Hulu series, if not doing much for the plot. Thankfully, the pace picks up after that. Fans of the show shouldn’t worry—this season finale doesn’t blow up the premise, but rather swaps one antagonist for another. “Chad Powers” isn’t a show like “The Good Place,” reworking its set-up at each break. It’s more of the same. CHAD POWERS – “8th Quarter” – Ahead of the team’s big bye week house party, Coach Hudson grows increasingly suspicious of Chad’s behavior. (Disney/Daniel Delgado Jr.) GLEN POWELL The same, and just as good, if not a little bit better, in round two. For one, the second season is funnier; there’s a bit with Russ’s dad ( Toby Huss ) in the “10th Quarter,” as the episodes are called, that is laugh-out-loud funny. Here, the jokes compound through a set piece that goes from jump-scare to hilarity to heart. Friend and accomplice Danny (Frankie A. Rodriguez) gets more character development this season. And it’s good to see Danny as an empowered version of the overly used gay sidekick: this is college, after all, and he’s not taking any of the bullying common on high-school shows. But it’s also frustrating that while multiple characters allude to his sexuality, we still don’t get to see him so much as make eyes at a love interest. In a show with countless poop jokes, surely some gay flirting wouldn’t be too grotesque, no? And of course, Powell’s charisma remains radiant. As wounded, asshole Russ, he’s handsome and terrible, continuing with his bad fashion and political choices, even as his search for real connection only grows stronger. As Russ-as-Chad, he’s awkward and nonsensical, but shares the same aching vulnerability. And it’s his journey that makes the show not just watchable but delightful, emphasizing the rewards of kindness and relationships amid off-the-rails kookiness. The silly does take up a lot of space, though.
